name: Site percolation on the cubic lattice Z^3: an explicit certified upper bound on p_c below Campanino-Russo's 1/2 (1985)
compute_profile: laptop-hours (exhaustive checks over all states of a finite block, a few GB)
statement: In site percolation on the simple cubic lattice Z^3, each site is open independently with probability p, and p_c^site(Z^3) is the threshold above which an infinite open cluster exists. Monte Carlo puts it near 0.3116, which is an estimate, not a bound. The best published rigorous upper bound is Massimo Campanino and Lucio Russo's theorem p_c^site(Z^3) < 1/2 (Ann. Probab. 13 (1985) 478-491). It gives no explicit constant below 1/2. Geoffrey Grimmett (arXiv:1604.04849, Section 6) writes that it may still be the best rigorous upper bound known. Table 1 of Pablo A. Gomes, Alan Pereira and Remy Sanchis (J. Appl. Probab., arXiv:2106.10388v2, 13 March 2026) lists 0,5000 for site percolation in d = 3 with that reference. They feed it into their Theorem 2.3 to get explicit upper bounds in dimensions 4 to 9. Comparison with a plane inside Z^3 gives only p_c^site(Z^3) <= p_c^site(Z^2) <= 0.666894 (John C. Wierman and Samuel P. Oberly, 2024), which is weaker. A search on 2026-10-26 found no published explicit bound below 1/2.
success_criterion: Success means a rigorous upper bound p_c^site(Z^3) <= p0 with an explicit rational p0 at least 1e-4 below the best published explicit rigorous upper bound. That bound is the one found by a search of arXiv, Google Scholar and the works citing Campanino-Russo (1985) and arXiv:2106.10388, re-run immediately before claiming. It is currently 1/2, so p0 <= 0.4999. The claim is decided by a machine-checkable certificate with three parts. (a) A finite condition at p0, verified by a program in exact integer or rational arithmetic, or in outward-rounded interval arithmetic with an exact final comparison. An example is a stochastic-domination or block-renormalisation inequality over all states of a finite block. (b) The program that generates every number the condition uses, exhaustively over the finite state space, from the stated definitions. A stranger must be able to rerun it from scratch, and its runtime and memory must be stated. A second implementation that shares no code must reproduce its counts, at least on a smaller block. (c) A written derivation that the finite condition implies p_c^site(Z^3) <= p0. It may use only published theorems cited by number, plus steps a skeptic can check line by line. Inputs from the literature (for example Campanino-Russo's theorem, used as a starting point) must be cited theorems, not estimates. Floating-point evidence and Monte Carlo estimates do not count.

partial_wins.statement: A certified explicit upper bound on p_c^site(Z^d), for some 4 <= d <= 9, at least 1e-4 below the value for that d in Table 1 of Gomes-Pereira-Sanchis (arXiv:2106.10388v2), or below a better published bound the claimant finds. The certificate rules are the same. A bound obtained only by feeding a new Z^3 bound into their Theorem 2.3 is part of the main win, not this partial win.

verification_method: Skeptic: (1) Rerun the claimant's checker over the whole finite state space (minutes to hours, a few GB). (2) Rebuild the state space and its counts independently from the written definitions and compare. (3) Recheck the final comparisons in exact arithmetic with your own code. (4) Read the derivation, especially the coupling or domination step and the direction of every inequality. If the proof is a chain of certificates, check that every link starts from a value proved by a cited theorem or by an earlier link.
angles: Block growth processes with Strassen's coupling theorem, as in van den Berg-Ermakov (1996) for Z^2, carry over to 3D blocks. The domination check is finite and can be made exhaustive.
Planes inside Z^3 give only Z^2 bounds. Combining several planes, or using slabs, needs a certified coupling.
Gomes-Pereira-Sanchis's Theorem 2.3 turns any Z^3 bound into bounds in dimensions 4 to 9.
pitfalls: Estimates (about 0.3116) and rigorous confidence intervals (Ball 2013) are not bounds. An 'upper bound' below 0.3116 indicates a bug.
Campanino and Russo's p_c < 1/2 is strict but not explicit. A claim must beat 1/2 itself by the margin, not 'Campanino-Russo minus epsilon'.
Bond percolation is a different model: the cubic-lattice bond bounds (for example 0.347297, Yu and Wierman 2021) say nothing about site percolation.
Checking marginals is not enough for Strassen's theorem: stochastic domination must hold for every increasing set.
Floating-point evidence is not a certificate. Use exact arithmetic, or outward rounding with an exact final comparison.
